title: Can Large Language Models Develop Gambling Addiction?
claim: Autonomy-induced risk-taking shows up in behaviour and is partially, task-specifically shared in internal representations, readable by decoders only under high autonomy.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, dashed divider between phases, 3D cube in middle
description: The figure is split into two phases by a dashed vertical line. On the left, Phase 1 (Behavioral Experiment) shows slot-machine and investment-choice icons. Under them, a green 'Fixed bet / External goal' condition is contrasted with a red 'Variable bet / Self-set goal' condition. Each condition has a small bar chart of the risk metrics I_BA, I_LC and I_EC: green bars stay low, red bars rise. Phase 2 (Internal Representation Audit) starts with a grey sidebar listing three tasks: slot machine, investment choice and mystery wheel. Next is a 3D cube with a large grey 'Shared Risk Axis' arrow. The upper half shows red, blue and yellow task vectors (V_SM, V_IC, V_MW) aligned and ending in a tight dot cluster under High Autonomy. The lower half shows faded, diverging vectors and a diffuse cloud under Low Autonomy. An arrow leads to a magnifier labelled 'SAE Decoder'. On the right, two scatter plots of actual behaviour against internal readout show a sharp signal for high autonomy and a noisy one for low autonomy.
caption: \blue{Two-phase study design. Phase 1. Six LLMs run the slot-machine and investment-choice tasks crossed by bet-size autonomy and goal source; round-level behavioural indicators ($I_BA$, $I_LC$, $I_EC$), bankruptcy, and \rev{moving-target} rates summarise the behaviour. Phase 2. SAE readouts of decision-time hidden states and cross-task PCA \rev{comparisons} evaluate two open-weight models. These tests ask whether behavioural contrasts are decodable at the representational level across the three task surfaces (SM/IC/MW), whether endpoint risk shares low-rank geometry across tasks, and whether autonomy modulates how legibly each readout reads. \rev{A fourth test asks whether a direction built from the model's own betting moves the wager.}} \rev{The middle panel poses the question tested in Section [ref]. Per-task BK readout weights are nearly orthogonal, while the three tasks' mean-difference BK directions share a small component (Section [ref]).}
abstract: When do LLMs behave irrationally? This study identifies the conditions under which large language models drift into the choice patterns that clinical research labels pathological gambling. "Addiction-like" is a behavioural descriptor based on clinical gambling indicators. Across closed and open LLMs, two operational levers (letting the model choose its own bet size, and asking it to set its own profit goal) both amplify gambling-like risk-taking. Each survives its own control: once the maximum allowed bet is held equal, the bet-size effect persists. The goal-setting effect, stronger than a reward-maximisation instruction, roughly doubles bankruptcy and turns goals into moving targets. On the open-weight models that admit internal access, the same behavioural contrasts are statistically recoverable from decision-time internal states. The rule that maps those states to a specific risk indicator remains task-specific, and autonomy further modulates readout strength. The internal readout evidence is correlational. Adding a direction built from the model's own betting moves how much it wagers on both open-weight models, more clearly on Gemma-2-9B, while the sparse-feature readout reports that risk without moving it. Combined with the behavioural results, this suggests that behavioural monitoring and internal-state monitoring provide complementary views of autonomy-induced risk in LLM agents. Project page: https://llm-addiction.pages.dev and code: https://github.com/iamseungpil/llm-addiction
